## Part A — Creating Vectors: c(), seq(), rep()

```{r}
scores <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
subjects <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")
scores[1:5]
subjects[1:5]

odds <- seq(1, 19, by = 2)
odds
seq(0,1, length = 5)

rep("A", 4)
rep(c("A", "B"), each = 2)
rep(c("A", "B"), times = 2)
```

##Part B: Subsetting (Accessing) Vectors

```{r}
grades <- c(88, 92, 79, 95, 84)
names(grades) <- c("Math", "Science", "English", "History", "PE")

grades [3]

grades[c(1, 4)]

grades [c("Science", "PE")]

grades[-c(1, 4)]

grades[grades >= 85]
```


5. Use negative indexing when you know an element is at the end of the data, even if you do not know its actual value or exact length. Use logical indexing when you want to filter data based on a specific condition rather than its position.

6. grades[10] returns <NA> instead of throwing an error so the code can keep running uninterrupted.

##Part C: Vector Operations and append()

```{r}
x <- c(1, 2, 3, 4)
y <- c(10, 20, 30, 40)

sum <- x + y
sum

multiply <- x * 2
multiply

z <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
short <- c(1, 0)

add <- z + short
add

fruits <- c("apple", "banana", "cherry")
append(fruits, "date")
append(fruits, "kiwi", after = 1)
```

8. The short matches the length of the z because it is longer by adding itself to every element on the z

9. Yes, because the length of the longer vector becomes a multiple of shorter vector.

##Part D — Lists: Creating and Subsetting

```{r}
student <- list(name = "Maria Santos", age = 20, grades = c(88, 92, 79), is_enrolled = TRUE)
student["grades"]
class(student[grades])

student[["grades"]]
class(student[["grades"]])

student$name

student[["grades"]][2]
```

10. A single bracket extracts a sub-list (preserving the list structure), while a double bracke extracts the actual value inside that element.

11. Vectors hold elements of the same data type, so subsetting with a single bracket returns a smaller vector. Lists, however, can hold complex objects like vectors and data frames. R uses double brackets to extract the actual object stored inside a list element, whereas single brackets just return a smaller list containing that element.

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
inventory <- list(item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"), price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00), in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]


inventory$item <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$item <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$item <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
inventory
```

12. It works because inventory$item and inventory$in_stock are parallel vectors of the same length. R first evaluates the logical condition on `inventory$in_stock` to get a TRUE/FALSE vector. It then uses those boolean values as a mask to filter `inventory$item`, keeping only the items at positions corresponding to TRUE values.

13. Relying on manual sorting risks misaligning the data, which ruins the structure and maps elements to the wrong items. To prevent this, group related vectors into a single data frame or list to keep the data bound together.

##Conclusion
Vectors hold elements of the same data type, making them ideal for calculations and sequences. In contrast, lists can bundle distinct objects—such as vectors and data frames—with different lengths and types. Use vectors for homogeneous data and lists for diverse or complex data structures.
